title: 🏎️The Fastest Kid in the Field
content:
I don’t remember the exact moment I fell in love with Formula 1. Maybe it was the sound, or the scream of engines slicing through corners like they were defying physics. Or maybe it was the precision, the way drivers danced with danger at 300 km/h and made it look like fun. Whatever it was, I was hooked early. Too early, maybe.

And it wasn’t just admiration. I genuinely thought I had the makings of a racer. I was fast. Not just playground fast, I mean fast. I used to be the quickest kid in my class, maybe even my whole section. I ran like my legs were built for it, like my body knew speed before my brain did. I’d race anyone, anywhere. Kids used to hesitate when I challenged them because they knew what was coming. I’d even give them a head start, let them begin halfway down the field, and still smoke them 😁. I ran so much, fell so many times, I had bruises on my legs and scrapes on my hands, but I didn’t care. I was a kid, what did I know? All I knew was that I loved the rush.

One day, my dad took me to a karting place. Not the fancy kind with telemetry and pit crews, but the kind where the cars were tethered to cables and the track was more arcade than asphalt. Still, I was hooked. The moment I pressed the pedal and felt the vibration in my hands, I knew this was it. Even if the cars couldn’t go fast, even if the steering was stiff and the track was tiny, I wanted more. And more. And more.

After that, I started watching racing religiously. I studied the legends like they were scripture Senna, Schumacher, Hamilton. I memorized circuits, learned race strategies, even practiced my own commentary in front of the TV. I begged my dad for an RC car, and after enough pestering, he gave in. It wasn’t just a toy to me tbh it was a machine. I raced it around the house, the yard, the street. I still have it, by the way. It’s beat up now, but it’s a relic of that obsession.

But where I was geographically, financially, realistically there was no path. No karting tracks down the street, no racing academies, no sponsors waiting to discover the next prodigy from my corner of the world.

It wasn’t just about not having access. It was the slow realization that no matter how much I wanted it, some dreams require more than passion. They demand infrastructure, connections, and timing. And I had none of those. and Well , I was a kid.

For a while, I didn’t just move on. I cut it off completely. No race weekends, no news, no headlines, no highlights. I didn’t want reminders. I didn’t want to feel like I was orbiting a dream I couldn’t touch. So I built distance. I detached. And honestly, it worked. The ache dulled. The obsession faded. I stopped thinking in lap times and championship points.

It took time to let go. Not in a dramatic way just gradually. Like sand slipping through fingers. I found other things to chase. b/c I’m an adult now.

But lately, I’ve started watching again. Just casually. A few races here and there. And it’s strange... there’s no sting anymore. Just a quiet flicker of what if. It doesn’t hurt. It doesn’t haunt. It’s just a reminder of how fiercely I can want something and how gracefully I can let it go.

But I still wonder...

title: 🍃The Quiet Confidence of Knowing
content:
Lately, I’ve been thinking about how rare and underrated it is to simply know what I’m doing. Not in the loud, boastful way. More like a steady hum beneath everything , a quiet confidence that I’m not just drifting. I’ve made choices, I’ve set things in motion, and even if the outcomes aren’t guaranteed, the direction feels right.

It’s strange how that matters. How knowing what I’m doing, even if it’s just for today, feels like planting seeds I might not see bloom for years. Maybe it’s not about certainty, but about clarity. I’m not fumbling in the dark. I’m walking with purpose, even if the path twists.

Does it matter? I think it does. Because the future isn’t some distant, abstract thing. It’s built from these small, intentional moments. And if I keep showing up with awareness, with care, with a sense of direction… then maybe that future will recognize me when I get there.

title: On Conviction
content:
Conviction isn’t loud. It doesn’t always come with fanfare or certainty. More often, it’s quiet—an inner steadiness that holds its shape even when everything else bends. And yet, it’s one of the rarest things to find in yourself.

We live in a world that rewards flexibility, adaptation, compromise. Those are valuable traits. But without conviction without a clear sense of what you stand for you risk becoming a mirror for everyone else’s expectations. You start to drift. You say yes when you mean no. You chase goals that aren’t yours.

Conviction doesn’t mean stubbornness. It means clarity. It means knowing what matters to you, even when it’s inconvenient. It means showing up for your values when no one’s watching. And it means believing that you deserve to live a life aligned with those values not just occasionally, but consistently.

You don’t have to be perfect. You don’t have to have it all figured out. But you do deserve conviction. You deserve to walk into a room and not shrink. You deserve to make choices that reflect who you are not who you’re trying to impress.

So if conviction feels far away right now, don’t panic. It’s not something you find overnight. It’s something you build, choice by choice, boundary by boundary, truth by truth. And every time you honor it, even in small ways, you get closer to the life that’s meant for you.

title: Reflection on Adaptability and Desire
content:
"if you can't get what you want, you teach yourself to want what you can get." At first glance, this phrase strikes me as both pragmatic and profound, but it also stirs a mix of emotions and thoughts.

On one hand, I see the value in adaptability. Life often throws challenges our way, and it's easy to feel frustrated when things don't go as planned. Learning to find contentment in what I have can be a powerful skill. It encourages gratitude and helps me focus on the positives in my life. This mindset shift can lead to greater happiness and fulfillment, as I start to appreciate the smaller things and recognize the abundance around me.

However, I also find myself questioning the implications of this perspective. Is it too easy to settle? While adapting is essential, I worry that this mindset might lead to complacency. What about dreams and ambitions? Should I compromise on my goals simply because they are currently out of reach? I think it's vital to maintain a balance between appreciating what I have and striving for what I truly want. 

It's important to remember that ambition drives growth. The desire to achieve more can inspire me to push my boundaries and explore new opportunities. Yet, if I become fixated solely on what I can't have, it can lead to disappointment and frustration. 

As I ponder this saying, I realize that the key may lie in the art of balance. I can teach myself to appreciate my current circumstances while still holding onto my aspirations. I can learn to want what I have, but not at the expense of losing sight of my dreams.

Moving forward, I want to cultivate a mindset that embraces both gratitude and ambition. I’ll strive to appreciate the present while also setting achievable goals that challenge me. It's a journey of self-discovery, and I look forward to seeing how this balance unfolds in my life.

title: Reflections on Ambition
content:
"Ambition is the first step to success. The second is action." – Unknown

This quote resonates deeply with me today as I reflect on the nature of ambition. It's a driving force that ignites passion and pushes me to pursue my goals. However, ambition alone isn't enough. It's the actions I take that truly matter.

I've realized that ambition can sometimes feel overwhelming. The pressure to achieve can lead to self-doubt and fear of failure. Yet, I've learned that it's essential to channel this ambition into tangible steps. Setting clear, actionable goals transforms ambition from a mere desire into a powerful tool for success.

Another thought comes to mind: "The future belongs to those who believe in the beauty of their dreams." – Eleanor Roosevelt. This reminds me that believing in my dreams is crucial. It's not just about having ambitions; it's about nurturing them with confidence and persistence.

Moving forward, I want to embrace ambition as a catalyst for growth. It's about taking calculated risks, learning from failures, and continuously striving for improvement. By aligning my actions with my ambitions, I can create a path toward fulfilling my potential.

title: No More Hollow Echoes
content:
Regret is a powerful teacher, but only if we choose to learn. Let the sting of past mistakes fuel your growth, not paralyze your spirit. Get stronger—not just in body, but in mind and will—so that you never have to revisit that hollow feeling again. Don’t be a senseless fool who squanders the hard-earned lessons life has handed you. Every experience, no matter how painful, holds the potential to shape you into someone wiser, sharper, and more resilient. Let regret be the spark, not the anchor.

You’ve already paid the price—don’t let it be for nothing. Channel that pain into purpose. Build discipline where there was once doubt, and clarity where confusion reigned. The past may have bruised you, but it doesn’t define you. What defines you is how fiercely you rise, how deeply you learn, and how boldly you refuse to let history repeat itself. Let every scar be a signature of strength

title: The Real Wealth Engine 🔩
content:
Cavemen had time, strength, and raw materials.  
So do we.  
The difference is knowledge.

Knowledge is the multiplier.  
It turns labor into craftsmanship, money into investment, and raw data into insight.  
It’s how we build products, services, and systems that scale.

Widely known knowledge creates competition.  
Unique knowledge creates leverage.  
It’s not just what you know, it’s what others don’t.

This is how civilizations rise.  
Not by accumulating more resources, but by learning how to use them better.

Knowledge compounds.  
It doesn’t wear out.  
It doesn’t rust.  
It builds on itself.

And when shared wisely, it elevates everyone.

title: The Symphony of Speed — Why Formula 1 Captivates the World
content:
Formula 1 isn’t just a sport — it’s a high-octane ballet of engineering, strategy, and human grit. Every race weekend unfolds like a drama: teams fine-tune machines worth millions, drivers push the limits of physics, and fans hold their breath through hairpin turns and split-second overtakes.

At its core, F1 is a relentless pursuit of perfection. The cars are technological marvels, capable of cornering at G-forces that rival fighter jets. The drivers? Elite athletes with reflexes honed to milliseconds and nerves of steel. But beyond the speed and spectacle lies a deeper allure: the stories. Rivalries like Senna vs. Prost, Hamilton vs. Verstappen, and the rise of underdogs like Brawn GP in 2009 remind us that Formula 1 is as much about heart as horsepower.

Whether you're drawn to the roar of the engines, the precision of pit stops, or the global glamour of Monaco and Singapore, F1 offers something for everyone. It’s not just racing — it’s a celebration of what humans can achieve when passion meets innovation.

title: 💭Learning How to Move 🐾
content:
So what am I actually doing with my life?

I’m probably in the darkest period I’ve ever faced, even if it doesn’t look that way from the outside. I say “probably” because I’ve learned how to hold myself together through tough situations, or maybe it’s not truly as dark as it feels. Still, most days I’m struggling just to move.

When I say “movement,” part of me pictures something grand: a big leap from point A to point B. But the sad truth is I know that’s not realistic. It would be foolish to believe I can rocket straight from here to there without taking the small, boring steps, because that’s simply not how life works.
The hardest part? I still don’t really know how to move, like a baby learning to crawl. I’m already 23 (well, I will be in about 17days), and I have almost nothing to show for it. This was supposed to be the time when I started taking care of my family. But Instead, I feel like a parasite.

For what it’s worth, this isn’t me whining like some emotionally unstable mess. I’m fully aware of what I’m saying, and I believe I’m saying the right things. There are definitely skills and qualities I lack, but I’m not even sure I can name them all clearly.

I like trying new things and learning. Maybe that’s exactly why I’m not excellent at any one thing yet. But I should be, because there are definitely people my age who are. There are guys out there enjoying their lives. Meanwhile I’m not really doing either.

It’s not even my main goal to be “happy”, I think happiness is a byproduct, not something to chase directly. What I am pursuing clearly isn’t getting me anywhere. And to make everything more urgent, I’ll be graduating in a month or so. Having some way to earn money is now critically important.

We grew up being told it’s all a system which goes like school -> high school → college → job → marriage → death. that path isn’t inherently bad. It only becomes terrible if I end up like my parents. stuck in a corporate job doing something I don’t enjoy just to survive. I’m not guessing; I’m sure if I could retire them tomorrow, they wouldn’t hesitate for a second. They do it because they have no real choice.

This was exactly the moment I was supposed to start lifting some of the weight off their shoulders, little by little, until I could become truly dependable and fully take care of the family.
I’m missing technical skills, soft skills, everything. I’m not “cracked” at anything, but I’m confident I can build whatever you throw at me. Except now… anyone can—with all the AI tools out there. Wishing for a rocket launch again instead of figuring out how to move even 1 cm.

I just want to see some kind of progress so I can tell myself I’m not completely wasting time, that what I’m doing actually matters.
I don’t hate anyone, but watching people around me run forward and make real progress isn’t enjoyable. I take it personally—because I should. No one else is going to hold me accountable except me.

I want to make a crazy amount of money!!! a lot of it.
So my friends have a truly dependable friend they can count on.
So my mom can buy whatever catches her eye when she’s out.
So I can help my dad with the house and everything else.
So my little sister never has to go through what I’m going through.
And most of all, so I can repay myself for all the blood and sweat I’ve already put in.
Even saying that feels hollow, because if I was really performing at the level I should be, I wouldn’t be writing any of this in the first place… right?
The path is simple, but it’s not easy.

It’s simple to break it down:

• Build many projects
• Get comfortable with dev tools, libraries, new technologies
• Land an internship (paid or unpaid) to prove I can add real value
• Start making money, because the more people know me, the more I become their go-to person for solving problems

But actually doing it? Not easy at all.
Even with what I already know, I’ve applied countless times. God knows how many rejections and ghosting's i had. I wish companies would just tell me what to fix. So far I’ve had exactly one interview. I thought it went great, my project seemed impressive enough even for an unpaid internship. Well Apparently not. I’ve heard nothing since.

If that one had worked out, it would have started the whole chain: experience → credibility → money → being dependable → helping family and friends → eventually running my own thing.
Goddamn it, I’m so ambitious.
But for God’s sake, what the hell am I actually lacking?

title: My Debts
content:
After seeing how much I was willing to sacrifice and how intensely I could move when there was a deadline, I realized something important about myself. I don’t even care now whether the result was good or bad. What stayed with me was how I was moving. That sense of urgency was all I needed. It made me sharp, focused, disciplined. It showed me how much I can actually achieve when the clock is ticking.

So the real question isn’t “Can I achieve big things?” It’s "Why does urgency only activate when someone else sets the clock?"

A school deadline has a clear date, clear consequences, and clear evaluation. You know exactly when it’s due, what happens if you fail, and how you will be judged. But life goals feel different. There is no fixed date, no immediate punishment, and no visible scoreboard. The brain prioritizes immediate threats and rewards, not abstract futures. That’s why I was sacrificing so much for something I don’t even look back at now, but not moving with the same intensity toward what I actually want out of this life.

I have learned from a friend that making things quantitative helps. Vague goals kill urgency. Saying “I want to be successful” does nothing. But saying for example “In six months I will ship two production-ready projects” or "By next month i would make my first $10k" welll this creates pressure. It creates measurement. It creates a scoreboard.

The truth is, my goals are not small... If anything, they are greater than the deadlines I once pushed myself for by miles. They shape the kind of life I will live and the kind of person I will become. There are people who will depend on me. There are responsibilities waiting for me. If I want to be dependable, capable, and strong, then I cannot treat my future casually. I have to take it seriously.

This is where the sense of owing something back comes in. I owe my parents. I owe my friends. I owe the people I will need to take care of... I’ve always felt that I would repay them somehow, but I never thought about it in numbers. Thinking of it as a literal debt changes something. It adds weight. It adds pressure. And that pressure is good. It makes it real. It turns gratitude into responsibility.

Deadlines work because they have consequences. So if life does not give me deadlines, I have to manufacture them. things like announcing publicly that I am launching something or telling a friend I will send them proof of progress every week. I can apply for something with a hard deadline. I can even commit money to something that forces execution, Because i can see how Pain creates urgency.

What I realized is that I am not incapable. I simply respond strongly to pressure. and the solution is not to wait for someone else to set the clock. but  to create one myself, attach numbers to my goals, make the stakes visible, and treat my dreams as obligations instead of options.

title: Vector Database
content:
Source article: [Encore Blog – “You probably don't need a vector database”](https://encore.dev/blog/you-probably-dont-need-a-vector-database?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

# What Even Is a Vector?

\`A vector embedding is basically a list of numbers representing meaning.

Example:

```txt
"cat" ->
[0.12, -0.88, 0.44, 0.91, ...]

"dog" ->
[0.10, -0.84, 0.40, 0.89, ...]
```

The closer two vectors are mathematically, the more semantically similar they are.

That means:

- `"cat"` is closer to `"dog"`
- `"car"` is farther away from `"banana"`

This is why vectors are useful for\
semantic search, recommendations, RAG , similarity matching, AI memory systems and such

# Embeddings

`Embeddings are vectors that are generated by an AI model. And i used `nomic-embed-text\`

taking the code of the vectors from first principles

### 1. Setup & Initialization

First, we set up `SearchKit` using the local Ollama embedder. Because like i said we are using a local model (`nomic-embed-text`)

```go
import (
    "context"
    "github.com/Yonathan-T/searchkit"
    "github.com/Yonathan-T/searchkit/embeddings"
)


// 1. Initialize the local embedder 
embedder := embeddings.NewOllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text")

// 2. Initialize the vector database and pass in the embedder
db := searchkit.New(searchkit.IndexOptions{
    Embedder: embedder,
})
```

### 2. Performing a Semantic Search

With `SearchKit`, you don't need to manually embed your query. You just pass your raw text directly to the `Search` method, and the library handles the rest!

```go
query := "Tell me something about outer space"

// Search parameters: context, query string, k (number of similar search you want), useCosineSimilarity (boolean)

results, err := db.Search(context.Background(), query, 2, true)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatalf("Search failed: %v", err)
}

// Print the top results
for _, r := range results {
    fmt.Printf("Score: %.4f | Content: %s\n", r.Score, r.Content)
}
```

### 3. How the Query Gets Processed (Under the Hood)

So, what exactly happens when you call `db.Search()`? Here is the internal flow of the package:

1. **The Search Method**: Inside `index.go`, the library intercepts your raw query text and passes it directly to the embedder you attached during setup:

```go
// Inside searchkit/index.go

func (idx *Index) Search(ctx context.Context, queryText string, k int, useCosine bool) ([]SearchResult, error) {
    // 1. Convert raw text to vector
    queryVec, err := idx.embedder.Embed(ctx, queryText)
    // ...
    // 2. Perform the mathematical search
    return idx.SearchVector(queryVec, k, useCosine), nil
}
```

2. **The Ollama API Call**: The `Embed` function then packages your text into a JSON payload and makes a local POST request directly to our Ollama instance w/c is `http://localhost:11434/api/embed`.

3. **Returning the Vector**: Ollama processes the text through the `nomic-embed-text` model and returns a `vector.Vector` (which is a `[]float64` slice of numbers).

4. **Distance Calculation**: Finally, `SearchVector()` takes that slice of numbers and compares it against every document in the database using either **Cosine Similarity** or **Euclidean Distance** to find the closest matches.

### 4. Database Schema

If you ever decide to persist these vectors in a production database like PostgreSQL (using `pgvector`), you'll need to define the exact dimensions of the model. Since the lil light model we used (`nomic-embed-text`) outputs 768 dimensions, your SQL would look like this:

```sql
-- Note: nomic-embed-text generates 768-dimensional vectors
embedding vector(768)
```

---

# Semantic Search

The difference between a Traditional search and a Semantic Search is the former `searches for keywords` so if it does not find the exact keywords it will fail while the later `searches for meaning` so its based on how similar is your query on meaning to the data we have in our DB.

For example in semantic search you might search for

```txt
"renewable power"
```

and that Query could find this since they are `similar`

```txt
"solar panels"
"wind turbines"
```

even if those exact words were never used. ([Encore](https://encore.dev/blog/qdrant-semantic-search?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Build a Semantic Search Engine with Encore.ts, OpenAI, and Qdrant – Encore Blog"))

# Similarity Search

The core idea of it all is, you are asking it to basically

```txt
Find vectors closest to the query vector
```

its usually done using this three algorithms `cosine similarity` , `euclidean distance` , `dot product`

# Cosine Similarity

It Measures angle similarity between vectors.

So the \`Closer angle the more similar meaning.

The formula for the angle is \\cos(\\theta) = \\frac{A \\cdot B}{\\|A\\| \\|B\\|}.

And In pgvector its simply

```sql
embedding <=> query_embedding
```

# pgvector

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds vector support directly into Postgres.

Enable it:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
```

Create table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE documents (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  content TEXT NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536)
);
```

---

# Why pgvector Is Interesting

The article's main argument:

> Most people don't actually need a dedicated vector database. ([Encore](https://encore.dev/blog/you-probably-dont-need-a-vector-database?utm_source=chatgpt.com "pgvector Guide: Vector Search and RAG in PostgreSQL – Encore Blog"))

Because with pgvector\
1 . vectors live in PostgreSQL\
2 . no sync pipeline\
3 . transactional consistency\
4 . simpler architecture (your docs and the embeddings live in the same table)\
5 . easier joins

# Dedicated Vector DB vs pgvector

Feature Dedicated Vector DB PostgreSQL + pgvector Extra service Yes No Sync required Yes No Transactions Harder Native Joins Limited Full SQL Complexity Higher Lower Best for Massive scale Most apps

# Typical RAG Architecture

RAG = Retrieval Augmented Generation

Flow:

```txt
User Question
    ↓
Convert question to embedding
    ↓
Search similar vectors
    ↓
Retrieve relevant docs
    ↓
Inject docs into LLM prompt
    ↓
LLM answers with context
```

---

# RAG Explained Simply

Without RAG the `LLM only knows training data` but with it, `it gets external documents at runtime` and that helps to reduce hallucinations , answer company-specific questions

# Example RAG Search Query

```sql
SELECT id, title, content,
       1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) AS similarity
FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector
LIMIT 5;
```

here the important part is this section

```sql
ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector
```

it means to sort by closest vectors

# IVF (Inverted File Index)

`partitions the vector space into clusters. At search time, only the clusters nearest to the query get scanned.`\
so it works by first grouping vectors into **clusters**.

Think of it like organizing books into shelves:

- Cluster 1 → sports
- Cluster 2 → science
- Cluster 3 → history etc

When a query comes in, IVF first asks:

> “Which clusters are most likely to contain similar vectors?”

Then it searches **only those clusters**, not the whole database.

# HNSW Index (Hierarchical Navigable Small World.)

builds a multi-layer graph where each vector is connected to its neighbors

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON documents
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```

the purpose is it have a faster nearest neighbor search, approximate similarity search , scalable vector retrieval

---
